newsitem.title: GERMANY: German share rally stutters, but seen resuming.
newsitem.headline: German share rally stutters, but seen resuming.

text.p: The German share market's powerful rally of recent days stuttered slightly in post-bourse trading Wednesday, but dealers said they expected the uptrend to reassert itself soon.
The IBIS DAX index, which tracks electronic dealings, slipped to 2,975.47 points, down 3.37 points, at 1413 GMT, down from the DAX's floor session close of 2,988.45.

"I would put this down to profit-taking," said a Munich dealer. "The market may have got a little overheated since Monday and we would need a little help from America to get things going again today."
Dealers said the cash market was also dragged lower by the futures market, with DTB March DAX futures down two points at 2,992.5.
Disappointment that the DAX did not vault the key 3,000 point mark, as many traders were targeting, had also introduced some insecurity into the market.
"We were just three points off in bourse trading and seem to have been weakening ever since. But that does not mean we will never get there," said a dealer.
Among blue chip stocks, decliners included Daimler-Benz AG, down two marks at 116.90 marks in afternoon dealings.
Daimler had been one of the stocks driven higher in early dealings by the dollar's ascent to a level close to 1.60 marks.
Chemical group Bayer also dipped from an early high of 62.93 marks to trade at 62.10, down five pfennigs.

BASF AG, which had soared in early trade to a high of 61.09 marks on the back of a report it later denied which said it planned to pay out dividends totalling more than one billion marks for 1996, was up 72 pfennigs at 60.20 marks.
Dealers said Wall Street's performance would likely give the German market its next direction.
There was some doubt as to how long the rally can last.

Commerzbank equity strategist Thomas Tilse told Reuters Financial Television: "This looks like the best of all worlds for German stocks and we will be testing the 3,000 level. But beyond that the outlook is quite bleak."
By the end of 1997, Tilse predicted the DAX would have dropped to 2,800 points. "Company earnings for 1997 are already priced into the market and I think realism will prevail."
Separately, WestLB predicted DAX company earnings would rise 16 percent in 1997 and slow to a 15 percent rise in 1998, although the DAX should reach 3,200 by the end of year.
